question: With their centuries-old tradition of self-management, solidarity and civic participation, Coimbra’s repúblicas, or student community houses, are a unique embodiment of the city’s academic and cultural life. They are more than mere student residences: these vibrant communities are woven into the academic history of Coimbra, rooted in the area classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The threat of eviction currently hanging over the República das Marias do Loureiro and the República Baco as a result of the university’s construction plans is just one example of a wider problem. Other repúblicas face similar threats to their continued existence and so to the preservation of this tangible and intangible cultural heritage. 1.
Is the Commission aware of this situation and of the cultural and patrimonial value of Coimbra’s repúblicas?
Does it think that EU financial instruments could be deployed to support the restoration of these buildings and, at the same time, to ensure the survival of the communities bringing them to life?
Is the Commission prepared to identify or make available EU funds for the safeguarding of this cultural heritage?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.11.2026) Cultural activities and engagement with Europe’s cultural heritage are core elements of the European way of life. The Commission is aware of the heritage value of the site and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO) recognition of the Coimbra’s university site and its continuing student traditions1.

Under Article 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the safeguarding and promotion of cultural heritage remain primarily a national responsibility. EU action is limited to encouraging cooperation and supporting or complementing national initiatives, in line with the principles of subsidiarity and conferral. The Creative Europe programme2 is available for the cultural and creative sectors.

While the programme is not designed to finance large-scale restoration works, heritage organisations may benefit where projects have a clear European cooperation dimension and fit the programme’s annual priorities and calls. The appropriate funding programme(s) can be identified through the CulturEU funding guide3.

Creative Europe supports networks such as Europa Nostra, which provides assistance to heritage buildings at risk. The 7 Most Endangered programme4 is currently open for candidate sites and includes funding, among other forms of assistance. Heritage is also being supported through other EU instruments.

The European Regional Development Fund5 finances heritage-related investments, in line with relevant cohesion policy programmes6. Also, the Centro 2030 programme can support the conservation and restoration of eligible classified cultural heritage. However, any proposal needs to meet the conditions of an applicable call and be selected by the relevant managing authority.
